title: Don't fall for the bulking meme
summary: NH argues that bulking is needed to grow, but that eating far beyond a modest surplus only adds fat. Rapid weight gain creates an illusion of progress because strength rises from fat and better leverage, which turns lifters into 'strength copers' stuck in endless bulk and cut cycles. He lists five signs of a failed bulk and three exceptions where aggressive bulking makes sense.
claims: Calories cannot turn into muscle; training creates the growth and the surplus only fuels recovery, while surplus calories beyond that become fat
Every successful bulk starts and ends in the gym; the kitchen is the easy part
A sizable but moderate surplus gets you about 95-98% of possible gains; doubling the surplus (e.g. 1000 instead of 500 kcal) does not double muscle gain, it just adds fat
He went from 110 to 210 lb by bulking slowly and conservatively; his years of eating big were the ones with the least muscle gain and the most fat
His best gains came on a lean bulk as a skinny teen fed by his parents, adding just a bowl of rice or some roast beef a day and gaining 10-15 lb of quality mass a year
Force-feeding an extra 1000 kcal a day tires you physically and mentally and can make you lethargic and fixated on diet instead of training
Increased calories during a bulk must coincide with increased training volume, workload and intensity, or the extra calories are simply stored as fat
Increase calories slowly and keep them stable until your bulking intake becomes your new maintenance (TDEE), which shows you gained muscle; only then raise calories again
Gaining 10 lb in two months versus five-six months may give the same bench increase, but the slower gain is much more likely to be muscle
Check the mirror as often as the scale when bulking; the scale number hypnotizes you into forgetting you wanted to look better
Strength progression is a valid sign of muscle growth only if the timeline is reasonable; strength gained from rapid fat gain comes mostly from better leverage and disappears when you cut
He bulked to 240 lb thinking he was big, cut to 210 and found the 30 lb he lost had been almost all fat
Sign of a failed bulk #1: the goal is to look big in clothes; natural lifters only fill out XL shirts by getting uncomfortably fat
Sign #2: citing absolute strength while ignoring pound-for-pound strength; adding 20 lb to the bench while gaining 20 lb of bodyweight means no real progress
Sign #3: coping with a poor physique by saying you are bigger than other guys; bodybuilding is building a statue, not piling up mass
Sign #4: picking a target bodyweight before the bulk (he wanted 225 from 180 to reach 100 kg) forces overeating; set a time frame instead of a number
Sign #5: you no longer like your body; a bulk should not make you hate what you see in the mirror
A slow or lean bulk is usually quality; a dirty or fast bulk usually gains mostly fat
Exception 1: performance-oriented lifters (e.g. Alpha Destiny) can bulk fast for strength if they track their old numbers at the same bodyweight
Exception 2: aesthetic lifters like Geoffrey Verity Schofield can bulk hard and cut if they track measurements before and after, but most people don't track data so it fails for them
Exception 3: very skinny lifters with fast metabolisms who stall on small surpluses should eat more aggressively, perhaps double; he only needs about +300 kcal
Endless 20 lb winter bulks and summer cuts with the same training create bulk-cut purgatory, stagnant strength and physique, and bad habits
